title: Independent components and projectile paths
learning_outcomes: Describe horizontal and vertical projectile motion separately when air resistance is negligible.
Resolve an initial velocity into horizontal and vertical components.
Explain and sketch the shape of a projectile path.
prior_knowledge_summary: Velocity includes direction and perpendicular directions can be treated with signed components.
Students can use constant-acceleration equations and maintain a sign convention.
Students can analyse one-dimensional vertical motion under constant downward g.
new_learning: Horizontal and vertical projectile motions happen at the same time but respond independently.
With negligible air resistance, horizontal velocity is constant and vertical acceleration is g downward.
Initial velocity components are u_x = u cos theta and u_y = u sin theta.
The combined motion forms a parabolic path.
not_yet_taught: Calculating total flight time and horizontal range.
Calculating impact speed and impact angle by recombining final components.
knowledge_boundary: Treat air resistance as negligible. Separate and describe the components, resolve the initial velocity and reason about path shape. Do not require full flight-time, range or impact-velocity calculations.

visual_rules.reason: Six varied visuals carry the spatial, component and path reasoning across the full teaching arc.
visual_rules.style: hand-drawn teacher sketches with only essential labels

blocks.title: Why does the dropped parcel move forward?
body: A bicycle moves steadily while a rider releases a ball. Predict where the ball lands relative to the bicycle if air resistance is negligible.
The ball keeps the bicycle's horizontal velocity while gravity changes its vertical velocity. It lands beside the bicycle, even though its path through the air is curved.

figure.purpose: Create the puzzle that one object can keep moving horizontally while falling.
figure.brief: Three-frame teacher sketch of a bicycle and released ball at equal time intervals, with ball and bicycle aligned horizontally and the ball dropping lower each frame.
figure.alt_text: A bicycle and a released ball move equal horizontal distances while the ball falls farther downward.

blocks.title: One motion, two independent stories
body: Ignore air resistance. No horizontal force acts after release, so horizontal acceleration is zero and horizontal velocity stays constant.
Gravity acts vertically, so vertical acceleration is 9.81 m s^-2 downward. Both component stories use the same clock, but a change in one direction does not cause a change in the other.

figure.brief: Split-panel sketch: horizontal panel with equal spacing and equal velocity arrows; vertical panel with increasing downward spacing and equal downward acceleration arrows.
figure.alt_text: Horizontal motion has equal spacing while vertical motion has increasing downward spacing under constant acceleration.

blocks.title: Write a separate line for each direction
body: Formula to remember for constant horizontal velocity: s = vt. Horizontally, s_x = v_x t. Here s_x is horizontal displacement in m, v_x is horizontal velocity in m s^-1 and t is time in s.

Formula to remember for constant vertical acceleration: s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2. Vertically, s_y = u_y t + \frac{1}{2}a_y t^2. Here s_y is vertical displacement in m, u_y is initial vertical velocity in m s^-1 and a_y is vertical acceleration in m s^-2.
Keep the lines separate. The only shared quantity is time.

figure.purpose: Model the two-column setup used before any projectile calculation.
figure.brief: Annotated two-column working layout labelled horizontal and vertical, with s_x = v_x t and s_y = u_y t + one-half a_y t squared, joined only by a small shared-time link.
figure.alt_text: Separate horizontal and vertical equation columns connected by the same time.

blocks.title: Split an angled launch before thinking about the path
body: A foam ball leaves a ramp at 10.0 m s^-1, 30 degrees above horizontal. Draw the velocity as the hypotenuse of a right triangle.
The horizontal component is u_x = u cos theta = 10.0 cos 30 degrees = 8.66 m s^-1. The vertical component is u_y = u sin theta = 10.0 sin 30 degrees = 5.00 m s^-1.
Cosine goes with the component next to the angle. Sine goes with the component opposite the angle. These are initial values, not two extra velocities.

figure.purpose: Make component resolution visible and prevent sine-cosine reversal.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn velocity triangle for 10.0 m s^-1 at 30 degrees, with adjacent u_x and opposite u_y, followed by the two substitutions.
figure.alt_text: A right triangle resolves an angled initial velocity into horizontal and vertical components.

blocks.title: Gravity does not use up horizontal speed
body: It can feel as if a falling object must slow horizontally because its path bends downward. That idea mixes the direction of the total velocity with the size of its horizontal component.

Gravity changes only vertical velocity. Equal-time snapshots remain equally spaced horizontally, while their vertical gaps change. The total velocity turns because one component changes while the other does not.

figure.purpose: Resolve the misconception using equal-time evidence.
figure.brief: Stroboscopic projectile dots with equal horizontal gaps, growing vertical drops and identical horizontal component arrows at every dot.
figure.alt_text: Projectile positions at equal times have equal horizontal spacing and increasing vertical separation.

blocks.title: Why the path curves into a parabola
body: Imagine two films played together. The horizontal film advances equal distances in equal times. The vertical film changes displacement with the square of time because of constant acceleration.

Combining those positions gives a smooth curve. A horizontal launch begins with a horizontal tangent and then becomes steeper. An upward launch first rises, has a horizontal tangent at its highest point, then falls. Under these assumptions the path is parabolic.

figure.purpose: Synthesize component motion into path shape for two launch types.
figure.brief: Comparison sketch of a horizontal launch and an upward angled launch, each with small component arrows and a marked horizontal tangent at the appropriate point.
figure.alt_text: Horizontal and angled projectile paths formed by constant horizontal motion and accelerated vertical motion.

blocks.title: Resolve first, then build the chain
body: A ball leaves a ramp at 18.0 m s^-1, 35 degrees above the horizontal.
Horizontal component: u_x = 18.0 cos 35 degrees = 14.7 m s^-1. Vertical component: u_y = 18.0 sin 35 degrees = 10.3 m s^-1.
After 0.80 s, horizontal displacement is x = u_x t = (14.7)(0.80) = 11.8 m.
Vertical velocity is v_y = u_y - gt = 10.3 - (9.81)(0.80) = 2.48 m s^-1 upward.
Keep 14.7 m s^-1 and +2.48 m s^-1 as separate signed components. Lesson 12 will recombine them into one velocity.

figure.purpose: Make the reasoning in resolve first, then build the chain visible.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn teacher-sketch summary with a positive axis, compact values, arrows, and only the labels needed for the reasoning.
figure.alt_text: Teacher sketch for resolve first, then build the chain.

blocks.title: Resolve the opening puzzle
body: The released ball stays beside the bicycle because both keep the same horizontal velocity. The ball alone accelerates downward, so its vertical position changes and its path curves.

Your new routine is: choose axes, resolve the initial velocity, write separate horizontal and vertical stories, use the same time, and combine only to describe the path. Next lesson will use that routine to calculate where and how a projectile lands.

concepts_taught: Horizontal and vertical projectile motions are independent but share time.
Horizontal velocity is constant and vertical acceleration is g downward when air resistance is negligible.
An initial angled velocity can be resolved into perpendicular components.
Constant horizontal motion combined with constant vertical acceleration produces a parabolic path.
misconceptions_addressed: The horizontal and vertical motions happen one after the other.
A curved path requires a horizontal force.
Sine and cosine components are extra velocities.
skills_students_can_now_use: Resolve an initial velocity into horizontal and vertical components.
State the acceleration and velocity properties of each component.
Sketch and explain a parabolic projectile path.
Set up separate component equations with a shared time.
resolve first, then build the chain
next_lesson_can_assume: Students can separate horizontal and vertical projectile motion.
Students can identify u_x and u_y from an initial velocity.
Students know horizontal velocity remains constant and vertical acceleration is g downward.
Students can use s = vt horizontally and s = ut + 1/2 at^2 vertically.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Students can calculate total flight time or range.
Students can recombine final velocity components into impact speed and direction.
Students can model projectile motion with air resistance.
